newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cold brings chaos to French rail and road traffic.
newsitem.headline: Cold brings chaos to French rail and road traffic.

text.p: Cold weather paralysed rail and road traffic in several areas of France on Friday and threatened to block skiers planning to return at the weekend from New Year holidays in the Alps.

Two German tourists, a man of 86 and a woman of 67, died from heart failures in separate incidents after buses they were travelling in were stranded overnight in the snows in the southeast, police said.
A 73-year-old man was found dead in a railway station in Mulhouse, in the Alsace region, bringing the death toll from the cold snap to 25 since it began on Christmas Eve.
The deaths of the German tourists occurred in the Drome region, where local officials urged people not to use their cars and a special disaster plan called ORSEC was put into action.
ORSEC allowed local officials in the area to call up extra police forces, paramilitary gendarmes and soldiers.
"The situation is serious," Drome prefect Jean Godefroid told French radio. "People must stop using their cars for their own safety."
Some 10,000 travellers were forced to camp overnight in trains, cars and emergency centres hastily set up after the freeze closed the rail link between Lyon and Marseille.

"We don't know when we will be able to reopen it," state railway SNCF chairman Louis Gallois told French television. "The current situation is an exceptional one. It only happens once every 20 years."
Ice built up to 10 centimetres (four inches) in diameter on power lines, halting high-speed TGV electric trains.
There was no rail traffic at all from Bordeaux on Friday and one section of the A10 motorway between St Andre de Cubzac, near the wine capital, and Poitiers was closed because of freezing rain.
Regional trains were running sporadically around Avignon, the Vaucluse and the Drome in southern France, often towed by diesel engines.
SNCF said it was doing everything possible to prepare for a flood of 30,000 to 35,000 travellers due to head home after New Year skiing holidays in the Alps.
"We are in a risk area for the next two days," said Alain Poinssot, SNCF director-general for clients.
Snow stranded up to 5,000 people overnight on the main A7 Autoroute du Soleil (Sun Highway). It partly reopened briefly south of Lyon on Friday but a few hours later it was closed again.
Police hoped that roads in the region could be cleared but the weather forecast said temperatures would not rise until Sunday.
Smaller airports ranging from Avignon and Valence in the south to Cherbourg in the north were closed by the icy conditions. France's biggest airports were open but operating with frequent delays.
Ice blocked many canals and chunks of ice cut off river traffic on the Loire river in western France. Oyster farmers worried that their produce could freeze to death on the way to market.

"It's Siberia!" the daily Le Parisien said. But it noted France was still far from the cold snaps of 1709, when more than a million people died of famine and epidemics, or 1880, when the Seine froze and the Invalides bridge collapsed into the river.
